topics.topic: Subjunctive after conjunctions (para que, sin que, antes de que...)
topics.explain: Some conjunctions always take the subjunctive because the action is not (yet) a fact: para que, a fin de que, sin que, antes de que, a menos que, con tal de que, en caso de que. Time conjunctions (cuando, hasta que, en cuanto, después de que) take the subjunctive only for pending actions; for habits and past facts, the indicative. If both clauses share the subject, use the infinitive: lo hago para ganar dinero. Watch out: antes de que needs the subjunctive even in the past: llegamos antes de que empezara.
examples: Te lo digo para que no te preocupes.
I'm telling you so that you don't worry.
Salió sin que nadie la viera.
She left without anyone seeing her.
Cuando llegues, llámame; cuando llegaba, siempre me llamaba.
When you arrive, call me; when she arrived, she always called me.

questions.q: Complete: «Te presto el coche con tal de que me lo (devolver) mañana.»
questions.why: Con tal de que ('provided that') always takes the subjunctive; with a present main verb and a future time, present subjunctive: devuelvas.

options: Llegamos antes de que empezara la reunión.
Llegamos antes de que empezó la reunión.
Llegamos antes de empezara la reunión.
Llegamos antes que empezó la reunión.
questions.why: Antes de que always takes the subjunctive, even when the event really happened; in the past, imperfect subjunctive: empezara.

topics.topic: Indicative vs subjunctive: opinion, doubt and emotion
topics.explain: Affirmative verbs of opinion and perception (creo que, pienso que, me parece que, está claro que) take the indicative: you assert something. Negated, they normally take the subjunctive: no creo que sea verdad. Doubt (dudo que), emotion (me alegra que, me molesta que, siento que) and value judgments (es importante que, es normal que) take the subjunctive. Watch out: es verdad / es obvio / es cierto que take the indicative, and in questions (¿crees que...?) both moods are possible.
examples: Creo que tiene razón.
I think she's right.
No creo que tenga razón.
I don't think she's right.
Me alegra que hayas venido.
I'm glad you've come.

questions.q: Complete: «No pienso que el proyecto (ser) rentable.»
questions.why: A negated opinion verb (no pienso que) normally takes the subjunctive: sea.
Expressions of certainty (es verdad que, es obvio que) take the indicative: es verdad que tiene razón. Emotion and doubt take the subjunctive.

topics.explain: After a preposition, Spanish uses article + que (el que, la que, los que, las que) or the more formal el cual, agreeing with the antecedent: la empresa para la que trabajo. For people, quien(es) also works: la amiga con quien viajé. The preposition must come before the relative; Spanish never leaves it at the end like English ('the friend I travelled with'). Cuyo means 'whose' and agrees with the thing possessed: la autora cuyas novelas traduzco. Watch out: don't drop the preposition (*la casa que vivo → la casa en la que vivo).
examples: Esta es la casa en la que nací.
This is the house I was born in.
La amiga con quien viajé vive en Lima.
The friend I travelled with lives in Lima.
Es un pueblo cuyos habitantes son casi todos jubilados.
It's a village whose inhabitants are almost all retired.

questions.q: Complete: «El editor ___ trabajo es muy exigente.»
questions.why: 'The editor I work for' = el editor para el que trabajo: the preposition goes before the relative. Para que means 'so that'.

questions.q: Complete: «La escritora ___ novelas traduzco vive en Bogotá.»
questions.why: Cuyo agrees with the thing possessed (novelas: cuyas), not with the owner. *Que sus is a common colloquial error.

topics.topic: Verbs of change: ponerse, volverse, hacerse, quedarse
topics.explain: English 'become / get' has several Spanish equivalents. Ponerse + adjective: a quick, often temporary change of mood or appearance (se puso rojo). Volverse: a deeper change of character (se volvió desconfiado). Hacerse: a change through effort or a gradual process, also with professions and beliefs (se hizo médico, se hizo rico). Quedarse: the state left after an event, often a loss (se quedó ciego, se quedó sin trabajo). Convertirse en + noun: transformation. Watch out: llegar a ser means 'eventually become' after a long process.
examples: Se puso nerviosa al ver la carta.
She got nervous when she saw the letter.
Con los años se volvió muy desconfiado.
Over the years he became very distrustful.
Se quedó sin palabras.
She was left speechless.

questions.q: Complete: «Cuando le hablaron del rumor, Esteban se ___ pálido.»
questions.why: A sudden, temporary change in appearance is ponerse: se puso pálido. Hacerse is for gradual or deliberate change; convertirse needs en + noun.

questions.q: Which sentence means 'After the accident he was left blind'?
options: Se quedó ciego después del accidente.
Se puso ciego después del accidente.
Se hizo ciego después del accidente.
Se convirtió ciego después del accidente.
questions.why: Quedarse describes the state left by an event, often a loss: quedarse ciego, quedarse sin trabajo. (Colloquially, ponerse ciego means 'to stuff oneself' or 'get wasted'.)

topics.topic: Lo + adjective and lo + adjective + que
topics.explain: Lo + masculine singular adjective turns a quality into an abstract idea: lo importante 'the important thing', lo mejor 'the best thing / part'. Lo + adjective or adverb + que means 'how + adjective': no sabes lo difícil que es 'you don't know how difficult it is'; here the adjective agrees with its noun (lo cansada que estaba). Lo de + noun means 'the business of': lo de la carta. Watch out: in this sense 'the important thing' is lo importante, not *la cosa importante, and 'how tired' after saber/imaginar is lo cansado que, not *cómo cansado.
examples: Lo mejor del viaje fue la comida.
The best thing about the trip was the food.
No te imaginas lo cansada que estaba.
You can't imagine how tired she was.
¿Te has enterado de lo de Esteban?
Have you heard about the business with Esteban?

questions.q: Complete: «No sabes ___ que son estas montañas.»
questions.why: Lo + adjective + que = 'how + adjective'; the adjective agrees with the noun it describes (montañas: bonitas).

questions.q: What does «Lo importante es que estás bien» mean?
options: The important thing is that you're OK.
It is important for you to be OK.
How important it is that you're OK!
The important person is you, and you're OK.
questions.why: Lo + adjective = 'the ... thing / what is ...': lo importante = 'the important thing'.

topics.topic: Passive voice: ser + participle, estar + participle, se
topics.explain: Spanish has three ways to express English passive ideas. Ser + participle (agreeing with the subject) presents an action, mainly in writing and the news, and can name the agent with por: el puente fue construido por los romanos. Estar + participle describes the resulting state: el puente ya está construido. Passive se is the everyday choice when no agent is mentioned: se construyó un puente. Watch out: English 'I was given a book' cannot become a ser passive (*fui dado un libro); use the active or se: me dieron un libro / se me dio un libro.
examples: La novela fue traducida por Daniela Ospina.
The novel was translated by Daniela Ospina.
Cuando llegamos, la puerta ya estaba cerrada.
When we arrived, the door was already closed.
Se venden pisos en el centro.
Flats for sale in the centre.

questions.q: Complete: «Cuando llegó el inspector, el informe ya ___ terminado.»
questions.why: The state resulting from an earlier action is estar + participle: ya estaba terminado. Fue terminado would describe the action itself.

questions.q: Which is correct for 'She was told the news'?
questions.why: Spanish cannot make the indirect object the subject of a ser passive. Use the active with an impersonal 'they' (le dijeron) or se le dijo.
